Sections.title: Month 1 Reflection
Sections.content:
>>For the first month of the project, a good portion of the first 2 weeks were spent discussing the logistics of the project such as project setup, environment setup, how pull requests will be handled, and what tech stack will be used. For the project management and collaboration, the team decided to use Trello as the means to handle all tasking required for the project. The alternative to Trello was Jira, but Trello was chosen because the team did not require the more advanced functionality that came with Jira, and since Jira took more setup time and was not free to use the team decided to use Trello instead. For pull requests (PR), the team decided to do a buddy system. What this means is that the team is split evenly into 2 sub-teams. One team will be handling the front-end (Justin and Bryan) and another team will be handling the back-end (Grant and Erich). When a team member makes a PR, they will ask for a review from their partner. In cases where a back-end team member needs to make changes to the front-end (or vice versa) in their PR, they will ask a member of the team for a review. The last of the project logistics that the team talked about was the tech stack. For this project, the team decided to go with a Vue, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL stack. Vue was chosen as the front-end framework primarily because of the customer. The customer primarily utilizes Vue in their projects and by having the application done in Vue, it will allow the customer to easily make updates to the application after it is passed on to them. A Python back-end was required for this project as most embedding projectors were made using Python. FastAPI was specifically chosen; it was primarily made for API, therefore having better performance and built-in documentation than alternatives like Flask. PostgreSQL was chosen because the team determined that a relational database was better than a non-relational database since structure was required for proper data analysis. PostgreSQL was chosen simply because it is the industry standard when it comes to relational databases. 
>>Concurrent with discussing project logistics, the team was also performing research on key components for the application such as embedding projectors and mapping library. In regards to embedding projectors, there were a few that the team had looked into. These were TensorFlow’s Embedding Projector, Voxel51’s FiftyOne, Renumic’s Spotlight, and Apple’s Embedding Atlas. In the end the team chose to go with Renumic’s Spotlight. This was for a variety of reasons but the main reason was Spotlight’s easy setup, well designed UI, and it had all of the functionality required for the project. Embedding Atlas was a close second to Spotlight because of its integration with JavaScript thus not requiring its own standalone web application. However, its lack of a 3D view caused the team to go with Spotlight instead. TensorFlow’s Embedding Projector was ruled out because despite having the best looking UI and containing all of the functionality the team was looking for, it was quite complex to setup and update dynamically using Python API. FiftyOne was ruled out for the poor looking UI and lack of 3D representation. For the mapping library the team had two options: MapLibre and Cesium. Of the two, the team decided to use MapLibre. The main reasoning behind MapLibre was that it was much easier to integrate than Cesium into Vue and had faster loading and rendering. Fast loading and rendering is very important in this application as the application could be displaying thousands of points at once. 
>>Towards the end of the month, the team began development on the application. With roughly 1 ½ weeks of development, the team was able to set up boththe FastAPI server andthe Vue application. The Vue application hasthe dashboard GUI completely set up withthe mapping library partially integrated. The FastAPI server has working routes and hasthe standalone Spotlight application up and running with some fake data in it.

Sections.title: Month 2 Plan
Sections.content:
>>For Month 2, the team plans to have a minimum viable product complete and a demo ready for the customer. To complete this, the team will need to have the database setup, integrate all of the various components into the front-end, and start setting up the front-end to retrieve data from the database via the back-end. 
>>In the front-end, there are 3 major feature additions that need to be done. These are the mapping component, the embedding component, and the timeline. The mapping component should use MapLibre to display all data from the database within a selected time range. Users should be able to select individual points which will highlight it and its respective embeddings within the embedding window. Users should also be able add pins at any point of interest. These pins should be saved within the database and loaded in whenever the user returns or refreshes the page. The embedding component needs to have the Spotlight web application integrated within it. The embedding components will need to hide as much of the Spotlight UI as possible leaving only just the embedding projector. The timeline component should allow the user to play through a timeline from the first data point to the last data point. As the timeline is progressing the data which both the embedding component and mapping component will need to update to show the data at the current time within the timeline. 
>>In the back-end, there are 2 core functionality that needs to be implemented. The first functionality that needs to be implemented is the ability for the back-end to be able to forward data tothe front-end. To do this,the back-end will have to establish a connection tothe PostgreSQL database and create GET routes forthe front-end to call. These GET routes will need to allowthe filtering ofthe retrieved data usingthe URL parameters. The other functionality that needs to be fully implemented is Spotlight. Whilethe Spotlight standalone application is set up and running, there are a lot of UI components that are unnecessary forthe project. The Spotlight standalone application will need to be cleaned up, removing as much clutter as possible. There also needs to be a way to updatethe Spotlight UI dynamically. This will be done usingthe Spotlight’s Viewer API.

Sections.title: Month 2 Reflection
Sections.content:
>>During Month 2, the team shifted its focus from planning and environment setup to active development and system integration. The primary objective for this sprint was to deliver a minimum viable product that demonstrates the core functionality of the application. By the end of the sprint, the team successfully implemented and integrated three major components: a map visualization, an embedding visualization, and a timeline filtering system. These components establish a functional pipeline from database to user interface and validate the decisions made in Month 1. 
>>The map component, developed using MapLibre, is capable of showing data points based on latitude and longitude values stored in the database. This confirms that the selection of MapLibre was appropriate, particularly due to its performance and compatibility with the Vue framework. The embedding component, powered by Spotlight, has been integrated into the application and is able to dynamically display data retrieved from the backend. Additionally, the timeline feature allows users to filter data based on time, with both the map and embedded components updating accordingly. This synchronization between components represents a significant milestone, as it demonstrates cohesive interaction between frontend and backend systems. 
>>Several design decisions were made throughout the sprint to address emerging challenges. One massive issue involved not having the timestamp data in the initial dataset. Since the timeline feature required Spotlight filtering with unix timestamps, this limitation needed to be resolved. After consulting with the client, the team updated the database schema and queries to include timestamp information. This ensured that the timeline functionality could operate as intended. Another consideration involved the capabilities of the Spotlight embedding tool. While Spotlight met most of the project’s requirements, its support for certain 3D features may be limited. The team decided to continue using Spotlight due to its overall strengths, with the understanding that any limitations could be addressed through alternative approaches in future development. 
>>The team encountered several challenges during this sprint. A significant obstacle was reduced development time due to three team members attending the Game Developers Conference in San Francisco. This resulted in the loss of one week of development time and required the team to adjust its workflow to meet deadlines. Despite this setback, the team was able to complete the MVP by increasing coordination and effort toward the end of the sprint. Another challenge involved refining the Spotlight interface. The standalone application contains several unnecessary interface elements, requiring additional work to tailor it to the project’s needs. 
>>From a project management standpoint, the team maintained consistent communication through scheduled meetings and ongoing discussions via Discord. Meetings held on March 17th and March 22nd were particularly important for assigning tasks and finalizing deliverables for the MVP demonstration. The team also continued to follow its established pull request review process, which contributed to maintaining code quality and consistency across the project. 
>>Overall, Month 2 represents a successful transition from planning to implementation. The completion of the minimum viable product demonstrates that the chosen technologies and system design are effective and capable of supporting the project’s goals. While challenges arose, the team adapted appropriately and remained on track for future development.

Sections.title: Month 3 Plan
Sections.content:
>>For Month 3, the team will focus on refining the minimum viable product and expanding its functionality to better align with client expectations. The primary goal is to transition from a functional prototype to a more polished and complete application. This will involve improving user experience, enhancing interactivity, and addressing technical limitations identified during the MVP demonstration. 
>>While the current integration of Spotlight is functional, it should be further improved to better the usability and visual consistency. The team plans to simplify the interface by removing unnecessary elements and changing the styling to better align with the overall application design. Additional UI will also be introduced to allow users to interact more effectively with the Spotlight data, including improved filtering and clearer visual feedback. 
>>The map component will also be expanded to include more advanced interaction capabilities. One planned feature is box selection, which will allow users to select multiple data points simultaneously. This enhancement will improve the analytical capabilities of the application and provide a more intuitive user experience. The team will also continue optimizing rendering performance to ensure that the application remains responsive when displaying large datasets. 
>>User interface and user experience improvements will be a priority throughout this sprint. While the MVP demonstrates core functionality, further work is needed to ensure a cohesive and professional appearance. The team will focus on improving layout consistency, responsiveness, and overall usability. This includes strengthening the interaction between components so that user actions in one part of the application are clearly reflected across the entire system, for example selecting a data point on the map highlights it in Spotlight. 
>>In addition to technical development, the team will incorporate feedback from the client following the MVP presentation with them on March 23rd. This feedback will guide final adjustments and help ensure that the application meets both functional and usability expectations. By aligning development priorities with client needs, the team aims to deliver a solution that is both technically sound and practically valuable. 
>>Based on current progress, the team is confident in its ability to meet the final product deliverable timeline. The successful completion of the minimum viable product indicates that the foundational components are in place, and remaining work primarily involves refinement and feature enhancement. With continued collaboration and effective task management, the team expects to complete all objectives for Month 3 and deliver a product that satisfies the project requirements.

Sections.title: Project Summary
Sections.content:
>>This project focused on developing a web-based visualization tool that integrates geospatial data with dimensional and time based embeddings. The work was completed in collaboration with Riverside Research and supported by their SWAT (Software Applications Team), which emphasizes rapid prototyping, design thinking, and agile development practices. The team worked closely with Chad Korbecki and Wes Baldwin.
>>The core problem addressed in this project was the disconnect between embedding visualization tools and geospatial mapping tools. While existing tools allow users to explore clusters in embedding space, they do not provide an effective way to connect those clusters to real-world geographic locations. This makes it difficult for analysts to understand how patterns in data relate to physical space.
>>To solve this, the team developed a full-stack application that links embedding visualizations with an interactive map and a timeline filter. The final product allows users to select data points on a map and immediately see their corresponding positions in embedding space, and vice versa. Additionally, users can filter data over time, with all components updating in sync.
>>By the end of the semester, the team delivered a fully functional system that demonstrates this integration. The application includes a customized embedding visualization tool, a performant mapping interface, and a backend capable of handling filtered data queries. While some limitations remain, particularly around large-scale data performance, the final product meets the primary goals of the project and provides a strong foundation for future development.

Sections.title: Project Background and Client Need
Sections.content:
>>Large amounts of data are often represented as embeddings, These embeddings are useful for identifying patterns, similarities, and clusters within data. However, in many real-world applications, especially those involving satellite imagery or sensor data, each embedding is also tied to a physical location.
>>The main issue is that most existing tools treat these two aspects separately. Embedding visualization tools, such as TensorFlow’s Embedding Projector, focus on mathematical relationships between data points but ignore their geographic context. On the other hand, mapping tools display spatial information but do not provide insight into the relationships between data points in embedding space.
>>Riverside Research identified this gap as a problem for analysts who need to understand both aspects at the same time. Without a unified tool, analysts are forced to switch between systems or attempt to mentally connect patterns across different visualizations, which is inefficient and prone to error.
>>The goal of this project was to bridge that gap by creating an interactive platform where embedding data and geospatial data are directly linked. Success was defined as building a system where selecting or filtering data in one view would immediately update the other views. 
>>Additional constraints included performance requirements, usability expectations, and the need to work within existing tools rather than building everything from scratch. The team was also expected to evaluate multiple tools and choose the best option based on extensibility and integration potential.

Sections.title: Project Narrative
Sections.content:
>>At the beginning of the project, the team focused heavily on understanding the problem and setting up a solid foundation. Early meetings with the client helped clarify the overall goal: to build a dashboard containing three main components (map, embedding visualization, and timeline). These initial discussions also provided insight into the expected end user and the types of data that would be used.
>>During the first few weeks, the team conducted research on potential tools and technologies. This included evaluating multiple embedding visualization platforms such as TensorFlow’s Embedding Projector, Voxel51, and Renumic Spotlight. At the same time, the team explored mapping libraries like Cesium and MapLibre. After comparing these options, the team selected Spotlight for embedding visualization and MapLibre for mapping due to their balance of functionality, performance, and ease of integration.
>>Once the core technologies were chosen, the team shifted into development. The frontend and backend were set up in parallel, with initial work focused on getting basic components running independently. This included setting up a Vue application, building a FastAPI backend, and running a standalone instance of Spotlight with sample data.
>>As development progressed, the team began integrating these components into a single system. One of the first major milestones was getting the map to display data points from the database. This confirmed that the backend and database were functioning correctly. The next step was embedding integration, which involved connecting Spotlight to the application and enabling it to display data dynamically.
>>The most important milestone came with the completion of the minimum viable product (MVP) at the end of month 2. At this stage, all of the three core components, map, embedding visualization, and timeline, were working together. Users could filter data by time, and both the map and embedding views would update accordingly. This demonstrated that the core concept of the project was viable and complete.
>>However, several challenges arose during this phase. One issue was the absence of timestamp data in the initial dataset, which was required for the timeline feature. This required changes to the database schema and coordination with the client to obtain the necessary data. Another challenge was reduced development time due to multiple team members attending the Game Developers Conference, which resulted in much less time for completing the MVP and in-turn led us to rushing and creating a few problems for future us to solve.
>>Following the MVP demonstration, the team shifted focus toward optimization and refinement, the two major things that were hurt from us rushing. A major area of concern was the performance of the Spotlight tool. Everytime you would change the time you are looking at on the timeline, Spotlight would reload, slowing down the whole application. To address this, the team decided to fork the Spotlight project and modify it directly. This allowed for removal of unnecessary UI components and improvements to how data was loaded and filtered.
>>Another key change during this phase was limiting the system to display only one day of data at a time. While this reduced the amount of data visible at once, it significantly improved performance and made the application more usable and stable.
>>Toward the end of the project, much of the work focused on integration and cleanup. While roles were initially divided between frontend, backend, mapping, and embedding, the final stages required more collaborative effort. In particular, ensuring that all components worked seamlessly together required adjustments across multiple parts of the system at once.

Sections.title: Technical Decisions and Design Reasoning
Sections.content:
>>One of the most important aspects of this project was selecting the right technologies. The team chose Vue for the frontend primarily because it aligned with the client’s existing systems, making it easier for them to maintain and add to the project after completion. Vue also provided a flexible and reactive framework for building the user interface.
>>For the backend, FastAPI was chosen due to its performance and simplicity. PostgreSQL was selected as the database because of its reliability and ability to handle structured data. Since the project involved geospatial queries, a relational database was a natural fit.
>>The choice of MapLibre over Cesium was based on performance and ease of integration. While Cesium offers more advanced 3D capabilities, MapLibre was easier to integrate into the Vue application and performed better when rendering large numbers of points.
>>The decision to use Spotlight was more complex. While it provided strong embedding visualization features, it also came with limitations, particularly in terms of customization and performance. Initially, the team attempted to use Spotlight as-is, but this quickly proved insufficient. The need to remove unnecessary UI elements and improve performance led to the decision to fork the project and create a custom version. This decision introduced additional complexity, as it required modifying third-party code. However, it ultimately provided greater control over the application and allowed the team to tailor the tool to their needs.
>>Another important design decision was limiting data to one day at a time. While this reduced the amount of information visible to the user, it was a necessary tradeoff to maintain performance. Attempting to load larger time ranges resulted in significant slowdowns, making the application difficult to use.
>>Overall, the team made decisions based on a combination of performance, usability, and project constraints. In many cases, tradeoffs were required, but the final system reflects a balanced approach that meets the core requirements of the project.

Sections.title: Final Product and Requirements Analysis
Sections.content:
>>The final product is a fully functional web application that integrates geospatial mapping with embedding visualization. Several key requirements were fully completed. The map component displays geospatial data and supports user interaction, including selecting individual points and groups of points. The embedding component dynamically updates based on user input and reflects relationships between data points. The timeline feature allows users to filter data over time, with all components updating in sync. The backend is capable of handling data requests and filtering based on user input, and the frontend provides a cohesive interface for interacting with the system.
>>Some features were partially completed or limited. For example, while the embedding visualization is functional, it does not fully support all desired 3D features due to limitations in the underlying tool. Additionally, performance constraints required limiting the amount of data displayed at once. A few planned features, such as more advanced UI interactions and extended data ranges, were not fully realized due to time constraints and technical challenges.
>>Despite these limitations, the final product meets the primary goals of the project. It demonstrates the ability to connect embedding data with geospatial context in a meaningful way and provides a usable interface for exploring that data.

Sections.title: Lessons Learned and Retrospective Analysis
Sections.content:
>>One of the biggest takeaways from this project was the importance of flexibility in software development. Many initial assumptions, particularly around tool capabilities, did not hold up during implementation. Being able to adapt to these challenges was critical to our team’s success. The team also gained experience working with third-party tools and understanding their limitations. In particular, modifying and extending an existing open-source project proved to be both challenging and valuable.
>>From a teamwork perspective, the project highlighted the importance of communication and coordination. While roles were clearly defined early on, the later stages of the project required more collaboration across different areas. This shift helped ensure that all components worked together smoothly.
>>Time management was another key lesson. External factors, such as reduced availability during certain weeks, had a noticeable impact on progress. This reinforced the importance of planning for potential delays and maintaining flexibility in a development schedule.
>>If the project were to be done again, the team would likely spend more time early on testing tools with realistic datasets to better understand their limitations. This could have helped avoid some of the performance issues encountered later and maybe have caused us to use different tools.
>>For future teams working on similar projects, it is recommended to prioritize integration and performance testing early in development. It is also important to be prepared to modify or replace tools if they do not meet project requirements.

Sections.title: Conclusion
Sections.content:
>>The Riverside Geospatial Embedded Projector project successfully delivered a system that integrates embedding visualization with geospatial mapping. While challenges were encountered throughout development, the team was able to adapt and produce a functional and meaningful application.
>>The final product demonstrates the value of combining different types of data into a single interactive platform and provides a strong foundation for future improvements. Overall, the project represents a successful capstone experience and a practical application of software engineering principles in a real-world context.
